analysis.one_liner: Bans partisan gerrymandering and mid-decade redistricting, excludes undocumented immigrants from apportionment, and adds new voting restrictions.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to three House committees in January 2026 with a single cosponsor and has seen no further action or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The FAIR MAP Act would require congressional maps to be compact, contiguous, and drawn without favoring a party or incumbent, and would bar states from redrawing districts more than once a decade unless a court orders it. It would also require photo ID for in-person voting, matching signatures for mail ballots, end same-day registration, ban ranked-choice voting in federal elections, and exclude undocumented immigrants from the census count used to divide up House seats and electoral votes starting in 2030.
analysis.who_benefits: Voters in heavily gerrymandered states would gain maps that are more compact and, in principle, more competitive, and no state could redraw its map repeatedly within a decade. Supporters of stricter voting rules would get a nationwide photo ID requirement and signature matching for mail ballots. States with few undocumented residents would be positioned to gain House seats and electoral votes after the 2030 census, at the expense of states with larger immigrant populations.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Voters in gerrymandered states; stricter-voting-rule supporters

how_it_helps.text: Requires every congressional district to be contiguous, compact, and not drawn to favor or disfavor an incumbent, candidate, or political party, and directs states to preserve cores of existing districts and political subdivisions like counties and towns.

Bars a state from redistricting more than once after each apportionment unless a court orders a new map to comply with the Constitution, the Voting Rights Act, or this Act, closing the door on repeated mid-decade map fights.

Requires a valid federal, state, or Tribal photo ID to vote in person, a matching signature for mail ballots, and registration before Election Day, which supporters present as safeguards for ballot integrity.

analysis.who_pays: Eligible voters without a government-issued photo ID, or who register on Election Day, would face new barriers to voting in federal elections. States with large undocumented immigrant populations would lose representation in the House and electoral votes under the 2030 apportionment, and every state would lose the option of ranked-choice voting or same-day registration for federal races. State legislatures would also give up their power to redraw maps whenever it suits them.
analysis.who_pays_short: Voters without ID, same-day registrants, immigrant-heavy states

drawbacks.text: The photo ID requirement, mail-ballot signature matching, and ban on same-day registration would make voting materially harder for eligible Americans who lack government ID, move frequently, or register close to Election Day, with no exception for hardship in the bill text.

Excluding undocumented immigrants from the apportionment count, and adding a citizenship-status checkbox to the census questionnaire starting in 2030, would shift House seats and electoral votes away from states with large immigrant communities and could discourage census participation, making the count itself less accurate for everyone.

Banning ranked-choice voting would force states like Alaska and Maine to abandon the federal election systems they have adopted, removing from voters a tool designed to reduce polarization and third-party vote splitting.

The anti-gerrymandering standards, such as compactness and not favoring a party, are loose and would ultimately be tested in litigation, with the bill routing all map challenges into federal district court.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The anti-gerrymandering provisions are a genuine, two-party reform: they would end the practice of legislatures redrawing maps repeatedly within a decade and require districts not drawn to protect incumbents or parties. But the bill pairs that reform with provisions that restrict how some eligible citizens vote (photo ID, no same-day registration, no ranked choice) and that shift political power between states based on citizenship status. The net effect depends on which provisions a reader weighs most; the bill bundles real pro-voter reform with real voting restrictions rather than being one or the other.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to three House committees, and nothing has happened since, with the current Congress running into January 2027.

narrative.text: Rep. Michael Lawler introduced the FAIR MAP Act in the House on January 22, 2026, and it was referred the same day to the Judiciary, Oversight and Government Reform, and House Administration committees.
The bill has one cosponsor, a Republican, and no committee action, floor action, or vote has been recorded since referral.

The current Congress runs through January 3, 2027, so the bill could still in principle advance, but bills referred to multiple committees with almost no cosponsors at this stage rarely reach the floor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: With no vote taken, the status quo holds: state legislatures and incumbent officeholders keep their ability to redraw congressional maps, including mid-decade, and no new voting restrictions have taken effect.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Status quo: legislatures keep map-drawing power, for now

for.name: Rep. Michael Lawler
for.what_they_did: Introduced the FAIR MAP Act on January 22, 2026, bundling redistricting limits, an apportionment change, and new voting requirements into one bill.

for.name: House Republican cosponsor
for.what_they_did: Signed on as the bill's only cosponsor.

against.name: House Judiciary, Oversight and Government Reform, and House Administration Committees
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral on January 22, 2026 and have taken no further action on it in the recorded history.

sides.party_line_note: Only Republicans are on record so far — a Republican sponsor and one Republican cosponsor — and no vote has occurred, so the partisan shape of any floor fight is unknown.

industries.industry: Major political parties and congressional incumbents
industries.note: The bill would strip parties and incumbents of their power to gerrymander and redraw maps mid-decade, cutting against their control. At the same time, the photo ID, registration, and ranked-choice bans would restrict voting options in ways that tend to concentrate electoral power with the two major parties.

industries.industry: States with large undocumented immigrant populations (e.g., California, Texas, New York)
industries.note: Starting with the 2030 census, excluding undocumented immigrants from the apportionment count would cost these states House seats and electoral votes, reallocating representation to states with fewer such residents.

industries.industry: Ranked-choice voting states and advocates (e.g., Alaska, Maine)
industries.note: The bill prohibits any ranked-choice system for federal elections, overriding systems those states' voters adopted and foreclosing the option for others.

analysis.trajectory: With a single cosponsor and referrals to three committees, the bill is very unlikely to get a markup or floor vote before the 119th Congress ends on January 3, 2027; most bills like this sit unheard and expire, or are reintroduced in the next Congress.
